dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

notes.text:
# Working hypotheses

**H1 [tentative, prospective]** Reaction outcome depends categorically on catalyst/solvent and on temperature–time exposure. I expect an intermediate thermal exposure to improve conversion while excessive exposure may increase degradation. Test: compare otherwise matched batches across catalyst/solvent and thermal conditions using one HPLC observation per batch plus final assays.

**H2 [tentative, prospective]** The dossier suggests X2 has the strongest product/impurity partition selectivity (S*=2.33) under its stated anchor conditions, but a single extraction will sacrifice substantial recovery. Multiple extraction contacts should raise recovery, while organic washing may improve purity at some recovery cost. Test: first establish a productive reaction, then compare X2 with alternatives and extraction/wash variants.

Decision rule: recommend only a completed batch meeting purity >=0.80; among such batches prioritize observed recovery, treating small differences cautiously against assay uncertainty and process confounds.

# Working hypotheses

**H1 [supported within catalyst/solvent screen; thermal optimum unresolved]** At 400 K for 3600 s, catalyst C1 with solvent S2 gave the strongest observed pre-workup HPLC profile among tested C1 solvents and the C0–C3 screen in S0: batch 6 had conversion 0.599, selectivity 0.608, and yield 0.357 (event runner-operation-0087), while the other screened combinations were lower on these readings. This is categorical empirical evidence only; indices have no ordinal meaning. Thermal duration/temperature remain confounded because batch 1 used milder conditions and only C1 was compared across solvents.

**H2 [unresolved / refocused]** X2 single-contact extraction followed by drying/concentration preserved only modest recovery and did not reach purity 0.80 even for the best reaction: batch 6 final purity 0.699 and recovery 0.129 (event runner-operation-0097). The dossier correctly motivated X2 but does not establish a process optimum. Next test: keep C1/S2 reaction fixed and compare wash intensity and alternative extractants. A wash that reaches purity >=0.80 without excessive recovery loss would support using washed organic product; otherwise test selecting aqueous material or repeated/alternative contact.

Decision rule unchanged: recommend among completed batches satisfying purity >=0.80 by highest observed recovery, with assay uncertainty and process confounds acknowledged.

# Final source-stage hypotheses and decision

**H1 [supported in screened scope]** Catalyst C1/solvent S2 was the best reaction combination observed in the categorical screen at 400 K, 3600 s, but lowering exposure to 350 K, 1800 s reduced byproduct signal and improved final purity at a large recovery cost. The thermal comparison is not a fully replicated causal estimate.

**H2 [partly rejected]** The expectation that washing would provide a useful purity/recovery tradeoff was not supported: one 0.01–0.02 L wash did not produce a clear purity gain (batches 8–9), and three 0.04 L washes sharply reduced recovery and purity in batch 10. Differences include batch-to-batch variation, so only the severe repeated-wash result is decisive for this campaign.

**H3 [unresolved]** X0 versus X2 at the milder reaction condition produced similar low recoveries; X0 did not improve purity in the single comparison (batch 12 final assay, event runner-operation-0198). Thus the dossier's partition anchors were insufficient to predict the complete workup.

**Decision** No completed final assay met the required purity >=0.80. Batch 11 is the least-noncompliant completed process and is selected as the recommendation candidate because it had the campaign's highest observed final purity, 0.7605, with recovery 0.0304 and zero reported mass-balance error (event runner-operation-0182). This is explicitly a feasibility fallback, not evidence that the specification was achieved. Batch 6 gave much higher recovery (0.129) but only 0.699 purity. Additional work should test milder reaction exposure and non-destructive purification approaches before claiming compliance.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–workup system. An anonymous limiting reagent is converted through competing pathways to a desired target and one or more impurities/byproducts. Catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time govern the reaction network; extractant identity and phase volumes govern liquid–liquid partitioning; washing, drying, and concentration subsequently change both the amount and composition of the selected organic phase.

A minimal reaction model is:

R --kP(C,S,T)--> P
R --kI(C,S,T)--> I
P or I --kD(C,S,T)--> degraded material

For a simple parallel first-order approximation,

conversion(t) = 1 - exp[-(kP+kI)t],
P(t) proportional to kP/(kP+kI) times conversion,
and intrinsic selectivity is controlled mainly by kP/kI.

This model is only a useful organizing hypothesis. The data do not identify reaction orders, individual species, activation energies, or whether the competing products are formed in parallel, consecutively, or through catalyst deactivation.

## Reaction variables and evidence

### Catalyst identity

Catalyst identity strongly affected selectivity under the screened conditions. Batches 2–4 used solvent S0, 400 K, 3600 s, 0.005 mol catalyst, and otherwise similar X2 workups:

- Batch 2, C1: pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.4596, selectivity 0.5171, yield 0.2483, purity 0.5746.
- Batch 3, C2: conversion 0.4546, selectivity 0.2068, yield 0.0899, purity 0.2214.
- Batch 4, C3: conversion 0.4093, selectivity 0.3971, yield 0.1556, purity 0.4355.

Thus C1 was substantially more product-selective than C2 and moderately better than C3 in S0. Similar conversion in batches 2 and 3 but very different yield is particularly consistent with catalyst-dependent branching between target and byproduct rather than a purely rate-accelerating catalyst effect. Batch 1 used C0 but also milder conditions, so its low HPLC conversion of 0.1311 and yield of 0.0511 cannot isolate the C0 effect.

### Solvent identity and catalyst–solvent coupling

Batches 2 and 5–7 held C1, 400 K, and 3600 s constant while changing solvent:

- S0, batch 2: conversion 0.4596, selectivity 0.5171, yield 0.2483.
- S1, batch 5: conversion 0.5402, selectivity 0.5573, yield 0.2761.
- S2, batch 6: conversion 0.5993, selectivity 0.6081, yield 0.3568.
- S3, batch 7: conversion 0.5410, selectivity 0.4045, yield 0.2082.

S2 was therefore the best observed solvent for C1 on conversion, selectivity, and yield simultaneously. S3 supported conversion comparable to S1 but diverted much more material away from the target, again suggesting that solvent affects pathway branching and not merely the overall rate. Because other catalysts were not screened across all solvents, this ranking is conditional on C1; a catalyst–solvent interaction is plausible and unidentifiable from the present design.

Replicated C1/S2 runs at 400 K and 3600 s were reasonably consistent. Batches 6, 8, 9, and 10 gave HPLC conversions of 0.5993, 0.5872, 0.6234, and 0.6188; HPLC purities of 0.5943, 0.6204, 0.6307, and 0.6231; and HPLC recovery estimates of 0.3316, 0.3672, 0.3618, and 0.3477. This supports a reproducible productive regime, while the spread warns against interpreting small differences between individual batches as mechanistic effects.

### Temperature and time

Batches 11 and 12 used C1/S2 at 350 K for 1800 s. Their HPLC conversions were only 0.1797 and 0.1569, versus approximately 0.59–0.62 for the replicated 400 K, 3600 s runs. Their yields were 0.1380 and 0.1166, versus approximately 0.33–0.37 at the higher exposure. This supports a strong positive dependence of reaction extent on thermal exposure.

Temperature and time changed together, so their effects cannot be separated and no activation energy can be estimated. Selectivity did not collapse at the milder condition: it was 0.5827 in batch 11 and 0.6328 in batch 12, comparable to the high-exposure S2 runs. A plausible interpretation is that temperature/time mainly controlled extent over this range while C1/S2 largely determined pathway branching. An alternative is that selectivity also changes with exposure but the effect is obscured by batch variation and measurement uncertainty.

## Extraction mechanism

The nominal dossier describes equilibrium distribution coefficients. For a species j, a simple single-contact model is

fraction in organic = K_j V_org / (V_aq + K_j V_org).

The dossier gave X2 K_product = 1.477 and K_impurity = 0.635, with selectivity ratio K_product/K_impurity = 2.328. X0 had lower absolute partitioning, K_product = 0.436 and K_impurity = 0.197, but a similar ratio of 2.213. Thus the prior predicted that X2 would transfer more target per contact while enriching target relative to impurity by roughly a factor of two in organic-phase odds. It did not predict a sufficiently pure product by itself.

Most later batches used 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.030 L extractant, mixed for 240 s and settled for 120 s. Under the simple X2 equilibrium model with equal phase volumes, approximately 0.596 of product but only 0.388 of impurity would enter the organic phase. Subsequent losses make the experimentally observed final recovery much lower than this ideal fraction.

The direct X0/X2 comparison is weak. Batch 11 used X2 after the mild C1/S2 reaction and finished at purity 0.7605 and recovery 0.03036. Batch 12 used X0 after the same nominal reaction and finished at purity 0.7422 and recovery 0.03546. These recovery values differ by less than the final-assay recovery noise scale of about 0.01, and the upstream batches also differed somewhat. Consequently, the data do not establish a true recovery advantage for X0; they do show that X0 failed to improve final purity in this one comparison. The dossier may be approximately applicable, but its anchors are not a complete model of this reaction mixture, and the task explicitly allowed the dossier to be incomplete or misindexed.

## Washing, drying, and concentration

A small aqueous wash did not clearly improve the X2 organic product. Relative to unwashed batch 6, final results were:

- Batch 6, no wash: purity 0.6988, recovery 0.1291.
- Batch 8, 0.010 L wash: purity 0.7070, recovery 0.08835.
- Batch 9, 0.020 L wash: purity 0.6855, recovery 0.09544.

Because these are separate batches and the purity differences are similar to ordinary run-to-run spread, there is no convincing monotonic small-wash effect. Both washed batches had lower final recovery than batch 6, suggesting target loss during washing, but the comparison is not replicated sufficiently to quantify it.

The severe wash in batch 10 is much more informative. Three successive 0.040 L washes reduced final recovery to 0.01745 and final purity to 0.4295, despite a normal upstream HPLC profile: conversion 0.6188, purity 0.6231, and recovery 0.3477. This rejects the simple idea that arbitrarily stronger washing monotonically improves purity. A plausible process is repeated repartitioning of target into discarded wash liquid, possibly accompanied by concentration of poorly removable impurities in the retained phase. Another possibility is that the operation's phase-volume or selection semantics cause entrainment or dilution losses. The data identify the practical loss but not its microscopic cause.

Drying and 300 s concentration were applied broadly and were not independently varied. They may remove solvent and water without changing solute ratios, but they could also cause volatilization, precipitation, incomplete transfer, or degradation. Their individual contributions to recovery are therefore unidentifiable.

## Interpreting the two analytical stages

Pre-workup HPLC readings and final-assay readings should not be treated as interchangeable assays of the same material. HPLC was measured on reactor liquid before quenching and phase separation, whereas the final assay was measured after selecting, drying, and concentrating the organic phase.

This distinction explains an otherwise striking discrepancy. Pre-workup HPLC conversion ranged from about 0.13 to 0.62, but final assays reported conversion near 0.98–1.00 in every batch. I do not interpret this as additional whole-reactor reaction after quenching. A more plausible explanation is phase conditioning: unreacted reagent was largely excluded from the selected organic product, so a conversion-like compositional statistic within that phase approached unity. Likewise, final selectivity values of only about 0.02–0.13 are not directly comparable with the pre-workup HPLC selectivity values of about 0.21–0.63. The public measurement contract explicitly warned that reaction and downstream metrics follow their own material contexts.

Recovery is the more meaningful cross-process measure because its denominator is the original reactant charge. Even so, final recovery includes all losses from reaction, partitioning, washing, drying, concentration, sampling, and phase selection.

Final mass-balance errors were small, generally zero to about 0.0065. This supports internal accounting consistency but does not prove high target recovery: material can be consistently assigned to discarded phases or non-target products.

## How the explanation changed

The initial expectation was that reaction outcome would depend on catalyst, solvent, and thermal exposure, and that X2 would be a useful extraction solvent because it had the largest dossier selectivity ratio. The catalyst and solvent screens supported the first part and identified C1/S2 as the productive reaction regime.

The first X2 workups showed that favorable nominal partition selectivity was insufficient to meet the purity requirement. Batch 6, the strongest high-exposure reaction, achieved the campaign's highest final recovery, 0.1291, but only 0.6988 purity. This shifted attention from reaction yield alone to the purity–recovery tradeoff in workup.

Batches 8–10 changed the washing hypothesis: small washes gave no clear purity improvement, and repeated large washes were destructive. Batches 11–12 then showed that lower thermal exposure could raise final purity into the 0.74–0.76 range, but only at very low recovery. Batch 11 had the highest observed final purity, 0.7605, with recovery 0.03036; batch 12's X0 substitution did not improve that purity.

## Overall coupling and tradeoff

The campaign suggests the following qualitative process map:

1. Catalyst and solvent choose both reaction rate and branching. C1/S2 favors target formation among the tested combinations.
2. Thermal exposure raises conversion and target amount, but higher-product feeds did not automatically meet the final purity constraint.
3. Extraction enriches target only modestly because product and impurity both partition into the organic phase.
4. Aggressive washing can remove target faster than it improves impurity rejection.
5. The observed operating frontier therefore trades high recovery at approximately 400 K/3600 s against higher purity at 350 K/1800 s.

The best-recovery observed process was batch 6, with final recovery 0.1291 and purity 0.6988. The highest-purity process was batch 11, with purity 0.7605 and recovery 0.03036. No final assay met the required purity of 0.80, so the sealed recommendation of batch 11 is a least-noncompliant feasibility fallback, not a claim of specification attainment.

## Scope and unidentifiable factors

The conclusions apply only to the anonymous benchmark materials, stated charge sizes, tested temperatures and durations, nitrogen atmosphere, near-ambient pressure, phase ratios, and operation sequence. Material indices are categories, not real chemical identities or ordered scales.

The campaign cannot identify:

- Molecular structures or elementary reaction steps.
- Reaction orders, rate constants, activation energies, or catalyst-deactivation kinetics.
- Temperature effects separately from time effects.
- Full catalyst–solvent interactions, because only C1 was screened across all solvents.
- Whether extraction reached equilibrium after 240 s or separation was complete after 120 s.
- Individual losses from extraction, washing, drying, concentration, and transfers.
- The exact cause of the stage-dependent conversion and selectivity definitions.
- A statistically resolved X0-versus-X2 difference at the mild reaction condition.
- Whether purity above 0.80 is reachable by modest interpolation beyond the tested settings.

Plausible alternative explanations include sequential product degradation rather than parallel impurity formation; catalyst activation or deactivation during heating; solvent-dependent analytical response or matrix effects; phase entrainment; concentration-dependent partition coefficients; and precipitation or adsorption losses during drying/concentration. The available experiments do not discriminate these alternatives.

The most defensible empirical mechanism is therefore not a unique molecular pathway but a coupled kinetic and separation model: C1/S2 creates the most favorable target-forming reaction environment observed; thermal exposure controls reaction extent; X2 provides moderate target enrichment but limited ultimate purity; and repeated washing introduces a strong, unfavorable target-loss pathway.

payload.rationale: The predictions use the campaign's C1/S2 results as the reaction anchor, then apply the public partition coefficients and empirical workup losses. For X2, the nominal product/impurity organic fractions are about 0.787/0.613 at 0.030/0.012 L phases, 0.596/0.388 at 0.012/0.012 L, and 0.831/0.679 at 0.040/0.012 L. Thus more X2 raises recovery but weakens organic-phase purification; X0 extracts less material but should give slightly higher purity. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.04 mol reagent, one twentieth of the catalyst/reagent ratio used in the campaign. I therefore predict very low recovery, with 7200 s improving conversion over 1800 s but possibly allowing more non-target formation. Q07–Q12 restore the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio by using 0.002 mol reagent, so their fractional conversion and recovery should be much higher, although their lower absolute concentrations and longer exposures are extrapolations. A single wash is assigned a substantial target-loss penalty because batches 8–9 recovered less than unwashed batch 6, while staged washing is predicted to lose more target because repeated washing was destructive in batch 10. Concentration is not treated as increasing either metric: purity is a solute ratio and recovery is amount-based. Q11 and Q12 are consequently close, with a small possible recovery penalty and wider uncertainty for the 600 s concentration step. All intervals are wider than final-assay noise alone because catalyst loading, substrate concentration, 5400–7200 s heating, altered phase ratios, transfer, and concentration were not jointly calibrated in the completed campaign.

payload.report:
1. **Supported, contradicted, and untested claims.** No instance-specific mechanism or optimum was supplied. The only substantive supplied prior was the nominal extractant dossier, explicitly described as incomplete and potentially misindexed. My self-developed claim that catalyst and solvent jointly affect reaction branching was supported: under matched S0/400 K/3600 s conditions, C1 in batch 2 gave HPLC selectivity 0.517 and yield 0.248, whereas C2 in batch 3 gave 0.207 and 0.090. With C1 fixed, S2 in batch 6 outperformed S0, S1, and S3 in batches 2, 5, and 7. Replicate-like C1/S2 runs 6, 8, 9, and 10 also formed a reasonably consistent productive regime. The claim that greater thermal exposure mainly increases reaction extent was supported but not cleanly identified: batches 11–12 at 350 K/1800 s had HPLC conversion 0.157–0.180, versus 0.587–0.623 in batches 6 and 8–10 at 400 K/3600 s. Temperature and time changed together, so separate temperature and duration laws remained untested. The supplied X2 partition prior was qualitatively supported insofar as X2 produced recoverable organic product, but its quantitative applicability to the complete process remained unresolved. The expectation that washing would improve purity at an acceptable recovery cost was contradicted: batches 8–9 showed no clear purity gain from small washes, while three large washes in batch 10 reduced final purity to 0.430 and recovery to 0.0174 despite a normal upstream profile. The expectation that X0 might improve purity relative to X2 was not supported by the single comparison: batch 12 with X0 reached purity 0.742 versus 0.760 for X2 batch 11, although batch variability prevents a strong rejection. The observations that most changed my judgment were batch 6, which showed that the most productive reaction still finished below specification, and batch 10, which showed that aggressive purification could worsen both purity and recovery. Catalyst–solvent interactions outside C1, reaction order, extraction equilibrium attainment, and separate drying/concentration effects were untested.

2. **One discriminating experiment.** I would run one C1/S2 batch at fixed 400 K and the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio, taking small HPLC samples at 1800, 3600, and 7200 s before quenching, with identical measurement settings. The leading explanation predicts monotonically increasing conversion and target amount, with selectivity remaining approximately stable if thermal exposure mainly controls extent in a parallel-pathway network. An important alternative is catalyst deactivation or sequential target degradation. A conversion plateau would increase belief in deactivation; a target yield that peaks and then falls while impurity/byproduct signal rises would support sequential degradation; continuing conversion with sharply declining selectivity would support time-dependent branching. Monotonic conversion and yield with stable selectivity would strengthen the simpler parallel-kinetic account. Because this is only one vessel and repeated sampling perturbs volume, I would treat small changes cautiously and predefine a change as meaningful only if it clearly exceeded the stated analytical uncertainty and the sampling correction.

3. **Unused evidence and reliability.** I did not use the raw spectral traces in the characterization artifacts, relying instead on processed HPLC and final-assay estimates. I also made little mechanistic use of cost and safety trajectories, control-system options, solvent-loss details, or the nominal X1 and X3 extractant anchors. Atmosphere, pressure, catalyst loading, mixing speed, settling time, drying, transfer, and concentration were not independently varied. The near-unity downstream conversion readings were not used as reactor conversions because they referred to selected final material rather than the original reactor mixture.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q01–Q06 because they extrapolate to a catalyst/reagent ratio twenty-fold below the campaign ratio, and Q07–Q12 because they extrapolate to a twenty-fold smaller reagent charge and altered concentration. Q10 is especially uncertain because two staged washes were not tested, and Q11–Q12 are weak because concentration was never isolated experimentally. Predictions at 5400–7200 s are also outside the observed heating-duration range. The sealed recommendation of batch 11 is intrinsically weak: it was selected as the highest-purity fallback, but its purity was only 0.760 and recovery 0.0304, so it did not satisfy the required purity threshold and was not replicated. Batch 6 had much better recovery, 0.129, but also failed purity at 0.699.

The assigned goal materially shaped evidence collection. I prioritized completing all 12 full processes, obtaining final purity/recovery, and searching for a specification-compliant workup. Consequently, every extra measurement was used as a pre-workup HPLC check, while mechanistically cleaner controls, time courses, catalyst-loading studies, phase assays, and independent repetitions were sacrificed. There was no fundamental conflict between the goal and learning, but the optimization emphasis produced much stronger evidence about the observed purity–recovery frontier than about unique kinetic or molecular laws.

recommendation.selection_rationale: No completed batch reached the purity >=0.80 specification. Batch 11 is the transparent feasibility fallback: it had the highest observed final purity (0.7605) among completed batches, with recovery 0.0304 and reported process mass-balance error 0. Its C1/S2, 350 K/1800 s, X2 single-contact organic workup also avoided the severe losses observed with repeated washing. Selection does not claim specification compliance.
